## Introduction

### Overview

In [w14a](../week14/w14a_quarto.qmd#recording-r-and-package-versions),
you saw how `sessionInfo()` **records** which versions of R and R packages you used.
That is useful information,
but it doesn't help you or anyone else **get** those versions back.

So far, you have installed all R packages in a single **personal library**:
a folder in your Home directory that is shared by all your R projects.
This works fine most of the time,
but has some downsides:

- When you update a package for one project,
  it is updated for all your projects,
  and code in another project may stop working.
- If someone else (or you, on another computer or a year from now)
  wants to rerun your code,
  they will install the latest versions of all packages,
  which may give different results or errors.

**renv** solves these problems by giving each project its own package library,
and by recording the exact package versions in a file that you commit to Git.
It is the R counterpart of the Conda environments and containers
that you have used for command-line software
(see [w6b](../week06/w6b_software.qmd) and the [Conda bonus page](conda.qmd)).

### Learning goals

On this page, you will learn:

- How renv works: project libraries, the lockfile, and the package cache
- How to set up renv in a project
- How to record and restore package versions
- Which renv files to commit to Git
- How to use renv with Quarto, `Rscript`, and Slurm batch jobs

## How renv works

renv adds three things to a project:

- A **project library** (`renv/library/`):
  a folder with the R packages for this project only.
- A **lockfile** (`renv.lock`):
  a text file that lists the R version and the exact version and source
  (e.g. CRAN or Bioconductor) of each package.
- An **`.Rprofile` file**:
  R runs the code in this file whenever it starts in this folder,
  and renv uses it to switch R to the project library.
  You'll learn more about what this means for running your code
  [below](#running-code-in-a-renv-project).

Installing the same packages again for each project would be slow
and take a lot of disk space.
Instead, renv keeps a **package cache** in your Home directory,
installs each package version only once,
and adds links to the cache in each project library.

## Setting up renv in a project

### Setting up a practice project

We'll first practice with renv in a new folder,
before you (optionally) use it in your Final Project.

1. In the terminal, create a folder `renv-practice` in your personal dir:

   ```bash
   mkdir /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/renv-practice
   ```

2. Open this folder in Positron (`File` > `Open Folder`).
   You need to do this,
   because renv only works when R starts in the project's top-level folder.

3. Create a Quarto document `analysis.qmd` with a code chunk that loads two packages:

   ```r
   library(ggplot2)
   library(here)
   ```

### Initializing renv

To set up renv in your project, run in the R console:

```r
renv::init()
```

<!---- TODO: If renv isn't installed in the personal library at OSC, add `install.packages("renv")` first. ---->

`renv::init()` does the following:

- It scans your code for the packages you use,
  such as those loaded with `library()`.
- It adds these packages, and the packages they depend on, to the project library.
  Packages that are already installed in your personal library are linked
  rather than downloaded again,
  so this should be fairly quick.
- It writes the lockfile,
  creates the `.Rprofile` file,
  and restarts R so that R uses the project library.

Take a look at the files that were created:

```bash
ls -a
```

Besides `analysis.qmd`, you should see `.Rprofile`, `renv.lock`, and `renv/`.
`renv.lock` is a text file in JSON format ---
open it to see what it records.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
#### Is renv active?
When R starts in a renv project,
it prints a message like `- Project '/fs/ess/...' loaded. [renv 1.3.1]`.
You can also run `.libPaths()`:
when renv is active, the first folder is inside the project's `renv` folder.
:::

## Recording and restoring package versions

### Installing packages and taking a snapshot

In a renv project, you install packages as usual,
with `install.packages()` or `renv::install()`,
but they go into the project library.
Install the _janitor_ package,
and add `library(janitor)` to your Quarto document:

```r
install.packages("janitor")
```

Installing a package does _not_ update the lockfile.
To see the difference between your project library and the lockfile, run:

```r
renv::status()
```

This should report that _janitor_ is used and installed, but not recorded in the lockfile.
To update the lockfile, take a **snapshot**:

```r
renv::snapshot()
```

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>What would happen if you took a snapshot after installing janitor, but without adding `library(janitor)` to your code?</summary>

By default, `renv::snapshot()` only records packages that your code uses
(and the packages they depend on).
So, _janitor_ would not be recorded in the lockfile.
That's usually what you want:
a package that you tried out but don't use doesn't need to be installed
by anyone who reruns your code.

</details>

A good routine is to run `renv::status()` and `renv::snapshot()`
whenever you have started using a new package,
and before you commit your code.

### Updating packages and going back

To update the packages in your project library, use:

```r
renv::update()
```

If everything still works, take a snapshot to record the new versions.
If something broke, you can go back to the versions in the lockfile:

```r
renv::restore()
```

### Bioconductor packages

renv can also install Bioconductor packages,
using a `bioc::` prefix:

```r
renv::install("bioc::DESeq2")
```

The lockfile then also records the Bioconductor version.
(Packages installed with `BiocManager::install()` are recorded too.)

## renv and Git

Commit these renv files to your Git repository:

- `renv.lock`
- `.Rprofile`
- `renv/activate.R`
- `renv/settings.json`

Don't commit the project library itself.
You don't need to add anything to your `.gitignore` for this:
renv creates a `renv/.gitignore` file that excludes the library and other local files.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
When you take a new snapshot,
commit the updated `renv.lock` along with the code that uses the new packages.
This way, your Git history records which package versions belonged to which version of your code.
:::

### Rerunning someone else's renv project

To rerun a project that uses renv, for example one that you cloned from GitHub:

1. Open the project's folder in Positron.
   When R starts, renv installs itself if needed.
2. Install the packages from the lockfile:

   ```r
   renv::restore()
   ```

renv records the R version in the lockfile, but it doesn't install R itself.
If your R version is different, renv prints a warning.
At OSC, you can see the available R versions with `module spider R`,
and it's a good idea to mention the R module you used in your project's README.

## Running code in a renv project

renv is only active when R starts in the project's top-level folder,
because that's where the `.Rprofile` file is.
Otherwise, R silently uses your personal library instead,
so your code may still run, but with different package versions.
Here's what that means in practice:

- **In Positron**, open the project's top-level folder,
  not a folder above it like your personal dir.
- **In the terminal**, run `quarto render` and `Rscript` from the project's top-level folder,
  also when the file you're running is in a subfolder:

  ```bash
  quarto render scripts/analysis.qmd
  ```

- **In Slurm batch jobs**, a job starts in the folder that you submitted it from,
  so submit from the project's top-level folder.
  The `render.sh` script from
  [w14a](../week14/w14a_quarto.qmd#running-r-in-a-slurm-batch-job)
  then works without changes:

  ```bash
  sbatch scripts/render.sh scripts/analysis.qmd
  ```

## Using renv in your Final Project

Using renv in your Final Project is **optional** ---
as the [rubric](../FP/FP4.qmd) says,
R packages can simply be installed as we did in class.
If you want to use renv:

1. Open your `FP` folder in Positron.
2. Run `renv::init()`, check the lockfile, and commit the renv files.
3. In your README, mention that the project uses renv,
   and that `renv::restore()` installs the packages.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
#### Check your `here()` paths
If you have been working on your Final Project with your personal dir open in Positron,
`here()` paths started at your personal dir,
like `here("FP", "data", "counts.tsv")`.
With your `FP` folder open,
`here()` starts at your `FP` folder instead,
because it contains a Git repository.
So, you would need to remove the `"FP"` part from such paths.
:::
